sections.p: You are a spice merchant. Stock your stalls with spices, sell full stalls for gold, and trade cleverly. Whoever has the most gold at the end wins.

Your hand is a caravan: the cards stay in the order they arrived. You may never rearrange it. New cards join at the back, and you must always stock from the front. Trading is the only way to get a card out of the middle.
You start with two stalls. A stall holds any number of cards of a single spice. On your own turn you may buy a third stall for 3 gold.
You must stock the front card of your caravan on a stall: one with the same spice, or an empty one. You may then stock the next card as well. If no stall fits, you first have to sell one.

Two cards from the deck are laid out in the market. Now everybody may trade with you, and only with you: caravan cards and market cards, in any numbers, gifts included. When you close the market, the cards still lying there go to you.
Every card received in a trade, and every market card you kept, must be stocked on a stall right away by its new owner. It never enters a caravan. Sell a stall if you need room.
You draw three cards to the back of your caravan. Then the next merchant's turn begins.

You may sell a stall at any time, even when it is not your turn. The more cards it holds, the more gold it pays (see the table). All its cards go to the discard pile. A stall with a single card can only be sold if none of your other stalls holds more than one.
The palace always demands one spice. Selling it pays 1 extra gold, provided the sale pays anything at all. Whenever the deck is reshuffled, the Royal Order moves to another spice.

When the deck runs out, the discard pile is shuffled into a new deck. The game ends once the deck has run out twice (three times with 4 or 5 players): the current round is played to its end so everyone has had the same number of turns. Then all stalls are sold. Most gold wins; on a tie, the longer caravan.
